study_identification.title: A neuroimaging measure to capture heterogeneous patterns of atrophy in Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies

clarity_of_research_objectives.reason: The study clearly articulates its research objectives in the abstract and introduction. The PICO elements are well-defined: Population (PD and DLB patients), Intervention (neuroanatomical normative modeling applied to T1w-MRI), Comparator (high vs low visual performers in PD; PD vs DLB; conventional GLM analysis), and Outcomes (total outlier count, dissimilarity patterns, associations with cognition). The study explicitly states three research aims: (a) investigating differences in total outlier count between groups, (b) comparing patterns of dissimilarity, and (c) evaluating correlations with cognitive severity.
clarity_of_research_objectives.supporting_text: We aimed to quantify patterns of neurodegenerative dissimilarity in participants with PD and DLB and evaluate the potential clinical relevance of total outlier count by testing its association with key clinical measures in PD and DLB... Here, we a) investigated differences in total outlier count between high and poor visual performers with PD; and between PD and DLB; and compared these to conventional cortical thickness analyses; b) compared patterns of dissimilarity between PD participants with high versus poor visual function; and between PD and DLB participants, and c) evaluated whether total outlier count correlated with cognitive severity in PD and DLB.

clear_definition_of_target_population.reason: The target populations are clearly defined with specific diagnostic criteria. PD patients were diagnosed using Queen Square Brain Bank PD diagnostic criteria, and DLB patients using the Dementia with Lewy Bodies Consortium Criteria (McKeith et al., 2017). The study includes detailed demographic characteristics (age, sex, education, disease duration) for each group. Control groups are also clearly defined with specific inclusion/exclusion criteria.
clear_definition_of_target_population.supporting_text: They were diagnosed as having PD or probable DLB if they satisfied Queen Square Brain Bank PD diagnostic criteria (Daniel and Lees, 1993) and the Dementia with Lewy Bodies Consortium Criteria (McKeith et al., 2017) respectively... We included 108 participants with PD (all from the UCL site); and 61 people with DLB (36 from UCL, 25 from the NACC site), plus 165 controls (38 from UCL, 127 from NACC)... Table 1 for demographic and clinical information

clarity_of_inclusion_and_exclusion_crite.reason: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are comprehensively specified for both sites. For UCL participants: exclusions include traumatic brain injury, major co-morbid psychiatric or neurological disorders, and dementia for PD patients (defined by Movement Disorder Society criteria). Controls had age range 50-80 and exclusions for neurological/psychiatric history. For NACC site, specific criteria are listed: dementia diagnosis, Lewy body disease as cause, not MCI, no PD diagnosis. The study also describes handling of potential outliers with detailed quality control procedures.
clarity_of_inclusion_and_exclusion_crite.supporting_text: Exclusions were a history of traumatic brain injury, or major co-morbid psychiatric or confounding neurological disorders; and for participants with PD, presence of dementia was also an exclusion criterion, defined using Movement Disorder Society criteria (Emre et al., 2007)... Inclusion criteria were being aged 50-80 and exclusions were the presence of past neurological or psychiatric history, or cognitive impairment on history or neuropsychological testing... Participants from site '8361' were included if they had a structural MRI scan and met the following criteria based on descriptors available in the NACC data file (06/2022 data freeze): 1) dementia diagnosis; 2) primary or contributing cause of cognitive impairment: Lewy body disease; 3) not classed as MCI; and 4) absence of a diagnosis of PD.

validity_of_normative_modeling_outcome_m.reason: The outcome measures are thoroughly defined and validated. The study clearly specifies: (1) brain measures used - cortical thickness (148 Destrieux parcellation regions) and subcortical volumes (21 regions), (2) normative reference cohort characteristics (n=58,836 from 82 sites), (3) deviation quantification method (z-scores relative to age- and sex-adjusted norms), (4) outlier threshold definition (z<-1.96, representing 95% confidence), and (5) aggregation method (total outlier count across 169 regions). The interpretation methods are also clearly explained, including sensitivity analysis with alternative threshold.
validity_of_normative_modeling_outcome_m.supporting_text: We generated z-scores from T1w-MRI scans for each participant relative to normative regional cortical thickness and subcortical volumes, modelled in a reference cohort (n = 58,836). Outliers (z < −1.96) were aggregated across 169 brain regions per participant... From the z-scores for each cortical and subcortical region generated from the normative modelling pipeline described above, outliers were defined as z-scores < -1.96. This is a commonly used threshold representing 95% confidence that points below it differ from the mean... The total number of outliers across the 169 regions (148 cortical and 21 subcortical) was summed per participant to provide the total outlier count.

handling_of_confounding_variables.reason: The study demonstrates comprehensive handling of confounding variables. Age and sex are incorporated as covariates in the normative modeling (warped Bayesian Linear Regression). Multi-site effects are addressed through: (1) accounting for site differences in the reference normative model, and (2) using adapted transfer learning approach to recalibrate the model with site-specific control data. All statistical analyses (linear regressions, group comparisons) adjust for age and sex. The different scanner parameters between sites (3T Siemens at UCL vs 1.5T GE at NACC) are explicitly acknowledged and handled through the normative modeling pipeline.
handling_of_confounding_variables.supporting_text: Rutherford and colleagues (Rutherford et al., 2022) modelled normative lifespan curves for cortical thicknesses across 148 regions (Destrieux parcellation) and subcortical volumes derived from Freesurfer using a warped Bayesian Linear Regression with age and sex as covariates, and accounting for site differences (Bayer et al., 2022)... The reference normative model was recalibrated to the study datasets with an adapted transfer learning approach (Kia et al., 2022). This involved inputting control data from our two study sites into the reference normative model to generate stable parameters for cortical thicknesses and subcortical volumes, to account for residual differences in data distributions, caused by factors such as scanner differences... Linear regressions, correcting for age and sex, were used to test for group differences

clarity_of_data_sources.reason: Data sources are explicitly identified and well-documented. Two sites are clearly named: (1) University College London (UCL) with the Vision in Parkinson's disease study (PI: Dr Weil, ethics reference 15/LO/00476), and (2) pseudoanonymised Alzheimer's Disease Research Center (ADRC) '8361' contributing to the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center (NACC) database with 06/2022 data freeze specified. Recruitment context is provided for UCL (National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery outpatient clinics, affiliated hospitals, patient support groups). The reference normative dataset source (Rutherford et al., 2022) is also clearly cited.
clarity_of_data_sources.supporting_text: Structural T1w-MRI data from two sites were used. The first site at University College London (UCL), included 108 participants with PD, 36 with DLB and 38 controls, from the Vision in Parkinson's disease study (PI: Dr Weil, Queen Square Ethics Committee reference 15/LO/00476). The second site was the pseudoanonymised Alzheimer's Disease Research Center (ADRC) '8361' which contributes to the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center (NACC) database (Beekly et al., 2007)... Participants from the UCL site were recruited from the National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery outpatient clinics and affiliated hospitals, or from national patient support groups

description_of_image_acquisition_protoco.reason: Image acquisition protocols are comprehensively described. For UCL: scanner manufacturer and model (3T Siemens Magnetom Prisma), coil type (64-channel head coil), sequence (MPRAGE), and complete parameters are specified: voxel size (1×1×1 mm), TE (3.34 ms), TR (2530 ms), flip angle (7°), acquisition time (9 min). For NACC site: scanner field strength (1.5T), manufacturer (GE), with reference to database for additional parameters. This level of detail allows for reproducibility and assessment of potential technical confounds.
description_of_image_acquisition_protoco.supporting_text: Structural T1w-MRI scans at UCL were acquired on a 3 T Siemens Magnetom Prisma scanner with a 64-channel head coil. Structural magnetisation prepared rapid acquisition gradient echo (MPRAGE) data were acquired using the following parameters: 1 × 1 × 1 mm voxel, TE = 3.34 ms, TR = 2530 ms, flip angle = 7°, acquisition time = 9 min. Structural T1w-MRI scans from NACC ADRC '8361' were acquired on 1.5 T GE scanners (further information on scanning parameters are available via the NACC database).

details_of_data_preprocessing.reason: Data preprocessing procedures are clearly and comprehensively described. The study specifies: (1) software and version (FreeSurfer v6.0.0), (2) specific processing pipeline ('recon-all' function), (3) parcellation scheme (Destrieux for cortical thickness with specific file names: lh.aparc.a2009s.stats, rh.aparc.a2009s.stats), (4) subcortical volume extraction (aseg.stats), and (5) detailed quality control procedures including visual inspection of grey/white matter boundaries and subcortical segmentation boundaries by a blinded researcher, with special attention to atrophied scans.
details_of_data_preprocessing.supporting_text: The 'recon-all' function in FreeSurfer v6.0.0 (http://www.freesurfer.net) was used to process all UCL and NACC MRI data. Cortical thickness values (Destrieux parcellation; lh.aparc.a2009s.stats, rh.aparc.a2009s.stats) (Destrieux et al., 2010) and subcortical volumes (aseg.stats) were extracted. Processed images were quality controlled by visually inspecting grey and white matter boundaries, and subcortical segmentation boundaries superimposed on the corresponding structural T1-weighted image by a researcher blind to clinical status. Particular attention was paid to atrophied scans which can sometimes affect robust segmentation of brain structures.

clarity_of_data_partitioning_methods.reason: Traditional data partitioning (train/validation/test splits) is not applicable to this study design. The study utilized a pre-existing reference normative model (Rutherford et al., 2022) trained on 58,836 participants from 82 sites. This reference model was recalibrated using control data from the two study sites via transfer learning, and then applied to patient data for generating deviation scores. The study design focuses on application of normative modeling rather than training/validating new models from scratch, making standard data partitioning procedures not relevant.
clarity_of_data_partitioning_methods.supporting_text: The reference normative model was recalibrated to the study datasets with an adapted transfer learning approach (Kia et al., 2022). This involved inputting control data from our two study sites into the reference normative model to generate stable parameters for cortical thicknesses and subcortical volumes, to account for residual differences in data distributions, caused by factors such as scanner differences. Z-scores were then generated for each individual with DLB or PD, per region, relative to the recalibrated reference values.

details_of_normative_modeling_approach.reason: The normative modeling approach is described in comprehensive detail. Key specifications include: (1) statistical model type (warped Bayesian Linear Regression with likelihood warping), (2) covariates (age and sex), (3) handling of multi-site effects (accounting for site differences), (4) reference cohort size and composition (58,836 participants from 82 sites), (5) brain regions modeled (148 cortical regions via Destrieux parcellation, 21 subcortical volumes), (6) transfer learning approach for recalibration (adapted from Kia et al., 2022), and (7) software/toolkit (PCNToolkit v0.20). The rationale for using warped Bayesian Linear Regression is also provided.
details_of_normative_modeling_approach.supporting_text: Rutherford and colleagues (Rutherford et al., 2022) modelled normative lifespan curves for cortical thicknesses across 148 regions (Destrieux parcellation) and subcortical volumes derived from Freesurfer using a warped Bayesian Linear Regression with age and sex as covariates, and accounting for site differences (Bayer et al., 2022). Bayesian linear regression with likelihood warping allows accurate modelling of non-Gaussian effects and upscaling of normative models to large cohorts (Fraza et al., 2021). Their reference cohort comprised 58,836 participants from 82 sites... The reference normative model was recalibrated to the study datasets with an adapted transfer learning approach (Kia et al., 2022)... All modelling steps were performed using PCNToolkit (v0.20) (Rutherford et al., 2022).

details_of_training_algorithm.reason: Training algorithm details are not applicable because the study did not train normative models from scratch. Instead, it utilized a pre-trained reference normative model from Rutherford et al. (2022) and applied transfer learning for recalibration. The transfer learning approach involved inputting site-specific control data to generate stable parameters accounting for site differences, but this is a recalibration process rather than model training. Since no de novo model training was performed, details such as optimization algorithms, convergence criteria, or training epochs are not relevant to this study.
details_of_training_algorithm.supporting_text: The reference normative model was recalibrated to the study datasets with an adapted transfer learning approach (Kia et al., 2022). This involved inputting control data from our two study sites into the reference normative model to generate stable parameters for cortical thicknesses and subcortical volumes, to account for residual differences in data distributions, caused by factors such as scanner differences.

model_performance_evaluation_metrics.reason: The study does not report normative model performance metrics. Standard metrics for evaluating normative models such as Mean Standardized Log-Loss (MSLL), Explained Variance (EV), Pearson correlation between predicted and observed values, Spearman correlation, or R² are not reported. The paper focuses on downstream applications of the normative model (group comparisons, dissimilarity analyses, clinical associations) but does not validate the model's predictive accuracy on the study datasets. While mean regional z-scores are reported in Table 1, these are descriptive statistics rather than performance metrics evaluating model fit.
model_performance_evaluation_metrics.supporting_text: No sections in the methods or results describe model performance metrics such as MSLL, EV, R², or correlations between predicted and observed values. The results focus on: 'Mean total outlier count was significantly higher in DLB... PD poor visual performers had significantly greater total outlier counts... Higher total outlier counts were associated with poorer MoCA...' but do not evaluate how well the normative model fits or predicts the data.

implementation_of_internal_validation.reason: The study does not describe internal validation procedures for the normative modeling pipeline. There is no mention of cross-validation, held-out validation sets, or assessment of model performance on internal data. While the reference normative model from Rutherford et al. (2022) may have been validated in its original publication, the current study does not report validation after transfer learning recalibration to the study sites. The focus is on applying the recalibrated model to generate z-scores for subsequent analyses, rather than validating the model's performance. Sensitivity analyses using alternative outlier thresholds are performed, but these test robustness of findings rather than model validation.
implementation_of_internal_validation.supporting_text: Methods describe recalibration and application: 'The reference normative model was recalibrated to the study datasets... Z-scores were then generated for each individual with DLB or PD...' No validation procedures or performance evaluation on internal data are mentioned. The sensitivity analysis with different threshold (z<-1.282) tests robustness of clinical findings but not model performance: 'to ensure our findings were not driven by a particular threshold, we repeated the analysis using a more liberal outlier threshold'

external_data_validation.reason: External validation of the normative model on independent datasets is not performed. While the study includes data from two sites (UCL and NACC), both sites' control data were used for transfer learning recalibration rather than for independent validation. The patient groups from both sites were analyzed together, and while subgroup analyses compared sites, these were exploratory analyses of clinical findings (e.g., DLB from UCL vs NACC showing different total outlier counts) rather than validation of model performance. True external validation would require testing the model on an independent dataset not involved in training or recalibration, which was not done.
external_data_validation.supporting_text: Both sites were used for recalibration: 'inputting control data from our two study sites into the reference normative model to generate stable parameters'. Subgroup analyses compared clinical outcomes across sites: 'DLB participants from the NACC site (n=25) had significantly higher numbers of outliers compared to those from the UCL site (n=36)' and 'subgroup analyses compared DLB participants at the UCL and NACC sites' - but these are not validation of model performance.

Additional supplementary tables detail PD subgroups (high/low visual performers) and site-specific comparisons. Missing data handling is implicitly addressed through sample size reporting.

performance_metrics_and_statistical_unce.reason: The study reports point estimates and measures of statistical significance but lacks confidence intervals. Point estimates are comprehensively reported (means with standard deviations for descriptive statistics; beta coefficients with standard errors for regression analyses). Statistical significance is appropriately reported with test statistics (t-values, W-statistics for Mann-Whitney U tests) and p-values throughout. However, confidence intervals or Bayesian credible intervals are not provided for key estimates. For example, group differences and associations are reported as 'β = -4.73 (SE = 1.30); t = -3.64; p < 0.01' but 95% CIs are not calculated or reported. This limits the ability to assess the precision of effect estimates beyond statistical significance.
performance_metrics_and_statistical_unce.supporting_text: Examples of reporting: 'Mean total outlier count was significantly higher in DLB (n = 61; mean = 8.7 (SD = 11.3)) compared to PD (n = 108; mean = 3.60 (SD = 6.0)) when adjusting for age and sex (PD versus DLB: β = -5.60 (SE = 1.74); t = -3.23; p < 0.01)' and 'total outlier count and both the composite cognitive score (β = -2.01 (SE = 0.79); t = -2.54; p = 0.02) and MoCA (β = -0.55 (SE = 0.27), t = -2.04, p = 0.05)'. No confidence intervals are reported for these or other estimates.

interpretation_specific_to_normative_mod.reason: The interpretation demonstrates strong understanding of normative modeling principles and their clinical implications. The study: (1) clearly explains the meaning of individual-level deviation scores and total outlier count as measures of overall neurodegeneration, (2) discusses the statistical threshold (z<-1.96) and its interpretation, (3) contrasts normative modeling advantages with traditional case-control approaches, specifically noting that 'conventional GLM group-average analyses did not reveal atrophy differences' while normative modeling detected differences, (4) discusses heterogeneity quantification via Hamming distance as unique to normative modeling, (5) addresses clinical significance through associations with cognitive measures, and (6) realistically discusses clinical application prospects and limitations. The discussion thoughtfully compares with alternative approaches (W-scores) and explains the benefits of the large reference cohort.
interpretation_specific_to_normative_mod.supporting_text: Total outlier count is agnostic to the regional location of cortical atrophy, whereas conventional GLM approaches require cortical atrophy to be in the same locations between individuals... Importantly, conventional GLM group-average analyses did not reveal atrophy differences between these groups... Neuroanatomical normative modelling is a recently established framework that maps individual patterns of variation from the expected norm (based on age and sex)... to quantify deviation from expected patterns... The number of outliers can be aggregated to provide the total outlier count, an individualised measure of overall neurodegeneration... Normative modelling has some key advantages over alternative approaches to quantifying atrophy relative to a reference group, for example using W-score metrics... The reference dataset of 58,836 used in normative modelling is around a thousand-fold larger than most W-score reference datasets, capturing much greater population variability

additional_comments.additional_comments: This study demonstrates excellent application of normative modeling to Lewy body disorders with several strengths: (1) comprehensive handling of multi-site data using transfer learning, (2) detailed quality control procedures with blinded visual inspection, (3) robust sensitivity analyses using alternative outlier thresholds (z<-1.282) that confirm main findings, (4) quantification of inter-individual heterogeneity via Hamming distance, (5) comparison with conventional GLM showing added value of normative modeling, and (6) careful handling of potential outliers with detailed clinical characterization (Supplementary Table 1). The supplementary materials confirm robustness across different thresholds and provide extensive clinical characterization. Limitations include: absence of model performance metrics after transfer learning recalibration, lack of confidence intervals for effect estimates, and limited explicit code/model sharing information. The study appropriately acknowledges site differences (1.5T vs 3T scanners, different disease duration, selection bias) and their potential impact. Reference: materials/1-s2.0-S2213158224000354-mmc1.md shows replication with liberal threshold and detailed supplementary tables.
